commenti.body: Great film and up there with the likes of Alien, Aliens etc. Aged so well, even better than the first Terminator where some of the special effects are concerned, and that came 2 years after

I believe The Thing was seen as something of an Alien knock-off when it came out but, yeah, it has really aged well. I think part of what makes it still very scary is the shape-shifting quality of the creature, as you imply. (The Alien franchies, by contrast, has really suffered in that regard.  We've all been saturated with images of the Xenomorph in every possible position, lighting setup etc. that there's no mystery left in its appearance. This was a huge source of the horror in the original Alien movie, IMO.) But I think part of why the creature in The Thing continues to frighten is the way its attempts to mimic its hosts produce a kind of "uncanny" feeling that has a very contemporary analogue in the various fails of AI imagery. (Think of the freaky hands with the wrong number of fingers that were common a few years back.)   
  
There is the horror of a creature attempting to imitate us and doing surprisingly well when it completes the job; then there's the horror of it not quite finishing the job and what that looks like - gory and gross; but then there's the horror of an intelligence so removed from human cognition that its very understanding of what "we" look like in the first place is so completely unfathomable it's terrifying. I think that for me might be the deepest level of horror in The Thing: the hint at a malign intelligence that's deeply unfamiliar to us.

I watched this for the first time this week, after reading great things I was excited to see it. I was disappointed 

I thought the setting, story, characters, acting, etc. were all pretty good. But the practical effects really took me out of the movie. It’s like the exact opposite of aliens/aliens and jaws. Those movies work because you don’t really see the monster very well, dark, partial shots, etc. The thing is the opposite, the practical effects are front and center, a major part of the movie. They looked really dated to me, pretty laughable I thought.

I like The Thing a lot overall, and this is kind of a specific complaint, but I was wondering if other people have the same issue.

A trope that annoys me in screenplays is when the audience needs to have certain information, but the writer cannot find an organic way for the characters to learn it, so it is simply guessed.  The Thing has one of the most ludicrous examples of that, when MacReady devises an absolutely insane and unmotivated theory that poking people's blood with a hot wire would have some effect and reveal who is a Thing.  Of course, this works perfectly so that the plot can continue, but it is such a laughable moment that it always takes me out of the film.
McReady explains that each separated part of the creature becomes a new creature and that  harming the newly created creature (the blood) would trigger it to defend itself.

If you enjoyed The Thing give the 1951 The Thing from Another World a watch, you'll be amazed at how many nods to the original there are in John Carpenter's remake. And then go and read the 1938 novella "Who Goes There?" that started everything.

Right, that's the half-hearted attempt to explain it, but he has no way to know that, and even if he did, no reason to think that would apply at a cellular level.  It works well for a set-piece, but it is just so silly from a story perspective.

This is over-analyzing a creature-from-outer-space movie, I know, it's just a moment that I always find sticking out in a mostly great film.
Haha I watched it a week ago for the first time as well. Wasn't hooked at all.

It’s not technically a remake, though. Same with David Cronenberg’s The Fly, or the Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1978) / Body Snatchers (1993) movies. People often miscategorize these as remakes when they are actually adaptations of their written source material. In the same way you wouldn’t call any subsequent film version of a Shakespeare play (say the 2015 film version of MacBeth) a remake just because that play had been adapted into a film previously.
